newsitem.title: CUBA: U.S. official sees increased pressure on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official sees increased pressure on Cuba.

text.p: A U.S. State Department official said on Tuesday that international pressure for political and economic change in Cuba had increased and was beginning to have an effect.
Michael Ranneberger, coordinator for Cuban affairs, told a news conference at the end of a week-long visit that one sign was what he called the "strident tone" of authorities.

He mentioned the "sending abroad of emissaries," an apparent reference to a current trip to central America by Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina to drum up opposition to the Helms-Burton law, a tightening of the U.S. economic embargo approved by Congress last year. Vice President Carlos Lage is in Uruguay with a similar message.

President Fidel Castro's government has engaged in a diplomatic offensive to draw attention to moves in the U.S. Congress to tighten the implementation of Helms-Burton. U.S. officials have said the moves would not represent a dramatic change in the Helms-Burton law.
Rannberger defended Washington's 35-year embargo against Cuba and said the policy of engagement followed by other countries had not been successful in gaining change.
"We're now seeing an increasing focus in the world for change in Cuba," Rannberger said. "The world is sending a more coherent message to Cuba."

He cited a "common position" on Cuba adopted by the European Union last December that requires change on the communist-ruled island before there could be improved relations. He added that several Latin American leaders had also begun to speak out for change.

The United States has sought to ease differences over Cuba after facing criticism of the Helms-Burton law, which was attacked by many allies because it provided for sanctions against third-country investors in Cuba.

During his visit, Ranneberger met with Foreign Ministry officials, members of the ruling Communist Party, dissidents and representatives of the Roman Catholic Church, as well as travelling to eastern and central areas of the island.

Earlier on Tuesday he inaugurated a $36 million, five-year refurbishment of the U.S. Interests Section building in Havana, which was built in 1953 and served as the U.S. Embassy until Washington severed diplomatic relations with Havana in 1961, two years after Castro's revolution.
Since 1977, when the two countries established interests sections in each other's capitals, the building has served as the U.S. Interests Section.
